This paper introduces a new class of models termed Temporal-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with exogenous variables (TV-PARX). These models extend the stationary PARX framework by allowing temporal parameters to evolve through a non-parametric smoothing approach. The resulting models offer enhanced flexibility in capturing time-varying mean structures, which is particularly beneficial for datasets exhibiting non-stationary behavior. We outline the methodology for estimating TV-PARX models and developing post-estimation inference procedures for both the smoothing parameter and the temporal parameters. Furthermore, we introduce a data-driven strategy to select the optimal order of the autoregressive and exogenous variables, as well as the optimal smoothing parameter. The efficacy of these methods is demonstrated using simulated data and a real-world dataset comprising daily counts of violent crimes in the United States over the past three decades. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive comparison of TV-PARX with other temporal variable models, highlighting its superior performance in forecasting and inference regarding time-series dynamics. The proposed approach is generalizable and applicable to any count data to investigate the sources of temporal non-stationarity. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/rohanrathod/TV-PARX. The atmosphere contains a mixture of gases and particulate matter known as aerosols, which significantly impact radiative forcing, air quality, and the performance of optical instruments like astrophotometers and space-based stellar surveys. While extensive research has been conducted to quantify aerosols for radiative forcing calculations primarily through satellite observations and atmospheric models—supported by ground-based networks such as AERONET, which utilizes sun photometers and Lidars—there has been relatively little effort to constrain these properties using stellar photometry for radiative forcing purposes. This is largely because the link between stellar variability and aerosol characteristics has not been sufficiently understood. However, given that approximately 90% of the data from photometric surveys like TESS, PLATO, and ZW come from this source, it is essential to develop methods for estimating atmospheric properties from such datasets. This paper reviews recent progress in constraining radiative properties using stellar photometry, with a specific focus on the efforts made by the MODIFIES project. These initiatives have successfully derived effective temperatures and vertical profiles of total optical depth (TOD) and Angstrom exponent (AE) from over 17,000 variable stars observed by ZW surveys, achieving a global root-mean-square error of 0.015 for the integrated TOD. Furthermore, we examined the trade-offs between using a single uniform aerosol model versus spatially varying models, finding that a single model is sufficient for constraining radiative properties when the goal is global energy budget calculations. Conversely, for applications requiring high precision in variable characterization—such as exoplanet research—spatially resolved models are necessary. We also analyzed the relationship between the second moments of the linear and quadratic Angstrom exponents and determined that the global root-mean-square error for the mean AE can be reduced by a factor of two if only the linear metric is employed. Finally, we briefly discussed future directions for this field. These constraints will also benefit other optical instruments, including astrophotometers and surveys like APOGEE, by providing additional data points for joint inversion models that aim to refine radiative property assessments. Such improvements are crucial for enhancing the precision of variable star characterization in astrophysics and for optimizing the use of astrophotometric data across other domains, particularly in atmospheric science. Ultimately, the techniques developed for this purpose could be adapted by other astronomical communities, such as helioseismologists, to extract physical properties from their own datasets. We introduce a simple yet potent enhancement to the standard Langevin dynamics algorithm, designed to accelerate sampling for systems with rugged potential energy landscapes. This improvement involves adding a friction-dependent term to the force applied along the reaction coordinate, effectively creating a "Ladderian" dynamics. By increasing the effective force along the reaction coordinate, the system accelerates across energy barriers, thereby reducing the time required to traverse them. Crucially, this modification preserves the invariant distribution, ensuring that samples remain representative of the canonical distribution. We validate this approach using the Adenine molecule, demonstrating a significant speedup of nearly an order of magnitude compared to conventional Langevin dynamics. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the acceleration achieved through this method. The Ladderian dynamics offers a straightforward and powerful alternative to other enhanced sampling techniques, such as metadynamics or umbrella sampling, for addressing the challenge of sampling across energy barriers. Furthermore, it serves as an efficient precondition for these methods, potentially yielding further performance gains. This study investigates how to leverage human-written image descriptions to evaluate automated systems, a task known as extrinsic evaluation. Unlike intrinsic evaluation, which requires no reference data, extrinsic evaluation aims to determine if human references can offer a more meaningful assessment of descriptive outputs than expected. The proposed method employs a neural network trained on a large collection of image pairs, each with two distinct descriptions, to generate a prediction for every image. This prediction serves as an intrinsic measure of variability between the automatic description and the human reference. By combining this variability metric with a standard extrinsic metric (BLEU), the approach creates a two-dimensional evaluation framework. This framework allows for the determination of a threshold where the intrinsic metric compensates for drops in the extrinsic metric, enabling the overall score to remain constant. Consequently, this combination provides a fairer evaluation of automatic descriptions by balancing the quality of the generated text against its alignment with the human reference. The authors term this approach the Variability-Adjusted Extrinsic Metric (VAX). Validated using two datasets, VAX demonstrates that the intrinsic variability metric correlates with both human judgments of quality changes and manual evaluations of edits made to automatic descriptions to match the human reference. Furthermore, when compared against other evaluation methods, VAX exhibits the strongest correlation with human assessments. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/rohitgupta99/VAX.

This study presents a simple prediction framework for the baryon and meson content of cosmic environments, specifically targeting the interstellar medium (ISM) and intracluster medium (ICM). The approach integrates the "missing baryon problem" with the concept of anomalous mesic charge carriers. It combines a standard mass budget for baryons and mesons with a novel model for the anomalous mass per unit charge of mesons. The resulting predictions align well with existing observations of baryon density and mass-to-charge ratios across a range of environments. These findings support the hypothesis that baryon content can be distributed between baryons and mesons, while the total charge density remains nearly neutral. Consequently, the conventional definition of baryon density must be revised to account for the presence of mesons. This framework offers a unified description of both baryon content and charge, applicable to individual astrophysical environments as well as the evolution of the universe. Fitting parton distribution functions (PDFs) demands a comprehensive theoretical framework that integrates diverse data sources, ranging from direct measurements to indirect ones derived via fitting procedures. This report outlines such a framework, detailing how to incorporate data processed through fitting steps. We present a unified framework capable of integrating all data types, including those obtained from prior fits. While this approach introduces additional uncertainties, it ensures consistency by utilizing the same theoretical structure for both direct data and those from earlier fits. We describe the implementation of this framework within the fastNLO code and demonstrate its application using a dataset from the LHCf experiment. Furthermore, we integrate data from other experiments that have been processed through previous workflows, such as the CT18 and MMHT2019 fits. The framework is also suitable for analyzing other data sources, whether direct or indirect, and can be employed to investigate the uncertainties associated with PDFs resulting from successive fitting procedures. Ultimately, this theory framework enables the incorporation of all available data types—direct and indirect—into a single global fit, thereby ensuring uniformity and consistency across the data selection. Such a unified framework is essential for generating PDF sets like the nXQCD family. To facilitate this goal, we have developed an open-source implementation of the framework in the fastNLO code, which is accessible at https://github.com/egavardi/fastNLO.

This study employs an active flame approach to simulate a gas jet fire subjected to acoustic excitation within a linearized framework. The research begins by detailing the construction of linearized boundary conditions designed to introduce acoustic waves into a turbulent jet flame. These conditions are derived using Reynolds-Averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) simulations, which also serve as the background flow model for simulating the flame's response to excitation. The simulations investigate a 30° conical jet flame, focusing on the influence of excitation frequency and Strouhal number on both global and local flame oscillations. Results indicate that global oscillation amplitudes initially increase with Strouhal number before peaking and declining, with the optimal strouhal number for maximum amplitude aligning with the first natural frequency of the specific geometry. Local fluctuations exhibit a complex spatial distribution, with the most significant variations occurring near the sound source and at the flame tip. Furthermore, the simulations successfully recreate the transition between axisymmetric ($n=0$) and first harmonic ($n=1$) global modes, as well as the emergence of local Kelvin-Helmholtz and tip vortex shedding instabilities. These findings are validated against experimental data regarding global oscillation amplitudes and local velocity fluctuations, demonstrating the model's ability to replicate key flame behaviors under acoustic forcing. Ultimately, this linearized active flame model offers a computationally efficient method for exploring flame responses to acoustic excitation and could be extended to assess reactions against other types of disturbances. Keywords: Turbulent jet fire; acoustic forcing; linearized framework; active flame method. (This abstract was created by the Artificial Intelligence (AI) assistant.)

Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a classical, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, formulated with the goal of creating a minimal nonlocal alternative to the theory of tetrads and connections required for regular nonlocal theories of gravity. This paper presents a detailed derivation of the NLG field equations. We demonstrate that a unique combination of constitutive and constitutive-like connections yields the expected nonlocal field equations when paired with a specific nonlinear function of the Ponce Tensor. Additionally, we outline a regularization approach for the NLG fields and provide a summary of their key characteristics. Ultimately, we establish the equivalence between the field equations of this nonlocal tetrad formalism and those of a corresponding nonlocal theory derived from a tensor formalism, offering a detailed analysis of the underlying nonlinear transformations.

Bipartite graphs represent a fundamental graph class with extensive applications in computer science, particularly in matching theory, graph coloring, and structural analysis. This study introduces a novel method for decomposing the vertices of a bipartite graph into two induced star forests. Such decompositions have significant implications for the chromatic index of bipartite graphs and their broader structural properties. Given that determining whether a bipartite graph $G$ admits a decomposition into two induced star forests is NP-complete, we propose an efficient fixed-parameter tractable algorithm based on the graph's feedback vertex set. Furthermore, we establish a tight linear-time FPT algorithm for this problem when parameterized by the size of a bipartition-conforming feedback vertex set. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms a direct FPT approach parameterized by the feedback vertex set. Additionally, we provide a linear-time solution for bipartite graphs where the chromatic index is at most twice the feedback vertex set. This work also explores the connection between decomposing bipartite graphs into two induced star forests and their chromatic index, offering a simple characterization for graphs with chromatic index exactly 3. The proposed method holds practical value for optimizing edge coloring in general graphs and their subgraphs. Our algorithm is implemented in C++ and accessible at https://github.com/Aniruddha-Bhattacharya/Bi-2ISF. Key terms: Bipartite graph, induced star forest, decomposition, chromatic index, and feedback vertex set.

This study introduces HyperDegrade, a system that prolongs the runtime of computationally intensive tasks by intentionally reducing CPU frequency, thereby extending battery life. Unlike prior methods that selectively deactivate CPU cores, HyperDegrade maintains all cores active while optimizing frequency selection. The proposed algorithm, termed HyperSlide, leverages historical workload traces to forecast future workload characteristics and dynamically adjust CPU frequency in real-time based on these predictions. Extensive evaluations using both real-world workload traces and simulated traces from the Million Instructions Per Second (MIPS) dataset demonstrate that HyperDegrade significantly enhances battery longevity compared to existing battery-saving techniques. Furthermore, the system effectively manages thermal constraints and fulfills real-time deadlines. Results indicate that HyperDegrade offers superior battery efficiency relative to previous approaches across various thermal limits and workload characteristics, with battery life improvements ranging from 1.15x to 1.27x.

This paper introduces a new procedure for classical and welded links, achieved by combining a crossing change with a full twist change. We demonstrate that this method enables unknotting for both classical and welded knots, as well as for classical and welded links. Furthermore, we establish an upper bound for the unknotting number (in the respective category) via this procedure. Additionally, we utilize this technique to simplify certain links, potentially lowering their unknotting number (within the corresponding category). As an application, we provide a negative result regarding the existence of a unknotting sequence of specific length for certain links in both categories. For classical links, this finding contradures a result by Conner, Grigsby, and Lackenby, whereas for welded links, it opposes a conclusion by Baadsgaard and Vendramin. Between the two unknotting operations available for welded links, we prove that switching the over/under orientation of a flype change is more effective than performing a full twist change. Finally, we apply this procedure to unknot several famous nontrivial links.

This study introduces a multi-stage game where two teams of autonomous agents strive to secure a map of urban streets. The game environment is influenced by the actions of an intelligent adversary who decides which intersections to block. We present a learning algorithm capable of finding an approximate Nash Equilibrium strategy for this tactical game. This strategy is derived without requiring explicit knowledge of the adversary's optimization method. The proposed algorithm is particularly useful for real-time applications, as it enables an agent to compute an effective response to an opponent's move on the fly. To develop this solution, we created a formal model of the game and designed a corresponding neural network-based learning algorithm. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated using a realistic urban map of San Francisco. Additionally, the paper details the specific neural network architecture employed for both the agent and the adversary. It concludes with a discussion of future research directions. This paper introduces a method for embedding a group acting on the Cartesian product of two sets into the wreath product of its respective groups defined on those sets. This approach, termed the Cartesian Partition Method, yields a constructive proof of a decomposition of a group into conjugate stabilizers of a Cartesian product of two points. When applied to additive groups of finite abelian groups, the Cartesian Partition Method offers a constructive proof of a decomposition of an additive group into a direct sum of two additive subgroups along with two automorphisms. Consequently, when used with finite finite-dimensional vector spaces over finite fields, the method provides a constructive proof of a decomposition of such a vector space into the direct sum of two subspaces and two linear transformations. The incorporation of this decomposition into the proof by the authors and K.  Edelman demonstrates that a group extending the symmetry of a vector space's automorphism and the additive group's symmetry of a specific direct sum decomposition of that vector space acts identically to a constructed group within the corresponding wreath product of the vector space's automorphism group and the symmetric group of order two. Furthermore, when applied to the partial linear spaces derived from the Cartesian products of projective lines, this decomposition enables an extension of the action of a group onto the symmetries of these projective lines' point sets. This analysis confirms the validity of the Riemann Hypothesis for the Cartesian products of projective planes of orders three through seven. However, the fundamental physics of the M\sagnac interferometer introduces a cutoff at high frequencies that limits the sensitivity of these Michelson-based sensors. This paper introduces a novel interferometric sensor utilizing an all-sagnac configuration designed to surpass the traditional Michelson and M\sagnac limitations at high frequencies. The proposed Michelson-sloshing-sagnac and all-sloshing-sagnac topologies offer enhanced sensitivity at high frequencies by leveraging wavepackets making repeated passes through the interferometer. We detail the optical layouts of both topologies, derive their frequency responses and noise spectra, and compare the primary and secondary diagonalized response spectra of the Michelson and sloshing-sagnac topologies against those of the CMZ topology (the conventional Michelson-sagnac topology). Furthermore, we present the sensitivity spectrum of a combined linear sensor network featuring a variable node linking the Michelson and sloshing-sagnac topologies. Finally, we outline the topological requirements necessary to detect gravitational waves in a tri-linear network comprising two sloshing-sagnac topologies and one Michelson topology. This paper addresses the non-intersecting visibility area challenge within the XL-MIMO stochastic access protocol. First, we establish the system model and formulate the optimization problem aimed at maximizing total visibility. Second, we propose a binary integer programming model to solve this problem. Third, we introduce a greedy algorithm to find a feasible solution. Finally, simulation results are presented to evaluate the proposed approach. These findings demonstrate that the binary integer programming method yields a higher total visibility area than the greedy algorithm, while also confirming that the greedy algorithm outperforms the XL-MIMO random access protocol. The results further indicate that the binary integer programming solution surpasses the greedy algorithm's output, validating the effectiveness of the proposed strategy in expanding the overall visibility area for an XL-MIMO system. This work confirms that optimizing the visibility area significantly enhances system performance, offering a viable alternative to traditional random access protocols. Although neural networks have largely supplanted $n$-gram models in modern language modeling due to superior performance, we demonstrate that simple $n$-gram models still offer significant advantages in specific scenarios. Focusing on the task of zero-shot text generation, we introduce a hybrid approach that leverages the complementary strengths of both neural and $n$-gram models. Our method employs a two-stage training process: first, we train a 3-gram model on the target domain to predict residual data alongside a Transformer-based transformer-33x model; second, we fine-tune the neural model using a combination of standard and 3-gram residual datasets. Evaluated across multiple languages at trigram, 5-gram, and 7-gram levels, our approach consistently outperforms existing methods. Specifically, our hybrid model achieves a 0.49% improvement over the strongest zero-shot baseline at the $t=3$ level and a 0.37% gain at $t=7$. These results indicate that simple $n$-gram models can effectively guide deep neural models, particularly in high-order predictions where neural models often struggle. Open-source code and models are accessible at: https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/Ngram-Residual-Neuro-Lang.

This study introduces Informed OCR (iOCR), a method that integrates manual tabulation with corrected OCR to process ballot images. Unlike conventional OCR, iOCR utilizes the context from already totalized sections of a ballot to enhance recognition accuracy in other areas. Experimental results demonstrate that iOCR significantly outperforms standard OCR on a real-world election ballot image dataset. The findings indicate that iOCR can achieve character-level accuracy surpassing 99%, a level of precision necessary for reliably automating the summation of vote counts on ballot images. Additionally, when applied to actual election ballots, iOCR corrects errors caused by degraded image quality, optical distortions, and recognition failures from conventional OCR. These corrections lead to more accurate vote tallies and reduce the time required for vote tabulation. The source code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/Aslam007/iOCR-Dataset. Keywords: OCR, vote counting, ballot image processing, elections, image processing.

This study examines global atmospheric circulation patterns in a 2D, differentially rotating, tidally locked terrestrial planet, utilizing a simple global circulation model. The planet features a uniform atmosphere and a zonally asymmetric, tri-pole differential rotation. By systematically adjusting the Rossby number, the Coriolis parameter, and the mass of the atmosphere, we identify distinct circulation regimes. Our findings indicate that the Rossby number and the atmosphere's mass are the primary drivers of these circulation patterns. Specifically, as the Rossby number decreases, the flow transitions from cyclostrophic to geostrophic. Furthermore, when geostrophic balance is achieved, the atmosphere exhibits a baroclinic instability characterized by the formation of eddies and zonal jets. We also observe that increasing the atmosphere's mass shifts the dominant circulation from equatorial super-rotation to poleward flow. These results align well with recent laboratory experiments on differentially rotating, tidally locked, gas giant planets. Additionally, our model offers a simplified framework for understanding atmospheric circulation in terrestrial exoplanets, potentially aiding in the interpretation of data from current and future direct imaging missions. The approach outlined here is applicable to a wide range of planetary atmospheres, including those of gas giants. To explore this further, a companion paper details the results for a planet with a zonally asymmetric, mono-pole differential rotation.

We introduce a novel hydrodynamic framework for classical and quantum fluids, termed the random hydrodynamic theory of phase-space quantum hydrodynamics (RHQHD). This approach extends the classical nonequilibrium statistical method of stochastic thermodynamics of hydrodynamics (NSTH) into the quantum domain by employing Wigner functionals. Within this theory, macroscopic fluid dynamics emerges as the average of microscopic linear quantum sound hydrodynamics, governed by stochastic quantum boundary conditions that generalize the Navier-Stokes equations. These stochastic quantum boundary conditions are derived from linear quantum kinetic theory using a closure scheme analogous to Grad's 13-moment method. The RHQHD model is derived from the collisionless Boltzmann equation for Wigner functionals, ensuring that all standard quantum statistical effects, including Bose-Einstein condensation, are naturally incorporated. Furthermore, this theory offers a nonperturbative description of nonequilibrium quantum systems, effectively accounting for both weak and strong quantum nonequilibrium behaviors. We specifically derive the boundary conditions for this theory from the Wangsland-Boltzmann equation for wave functional vectors, providing a unified derivation of both the boundary conditions and the bulk equations. As a practical application, we develop a simplified mean-field model to simulate shock waves in superfluids, yielding explicit boundary conditions for this model. Additionally, we establish a closure scheme for the theory of stochastic superfluid hydrodynamics, connecting it to the previously described mean-field approach. Finally, we outline the derivation of the corresponding linear response quantum kinetic theory and its boundary conditions, which can be applied to investigate thermal transport in superfluids. The RHQHD theory of Bose fluids is formulated within the Wick-Wigner formalism of quantum nonequilibrium statistics; a summary of the necessary mathematical foundations is provided in Appendix A. Key boundary conditions for various models are detailed in Section II, while Section III presents the mean-field theory of superfluids and its associated boundary conditions. Section IV covers the linear response theory of superfluids and its boundary conditions. Section V outlines the specific models and methods employed in this study, and Section VI summarizes our findings and discusses their implications. Using the AMPT model, we re-examed the connection between initial geometry and anisotropic flow in central Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Our analysis indicates that hydrodynamic evolution amplifies anisotropic flows, whereas non-equilibrium transport from the surface layers suppresses these flows. Specifically, non-equilibrium effects are the primary driver of the $v_2/v_1\perp$ ratio, while both mechanisms jointly determine the $v_3/v_1$ ratio. The observed suppression of $v_3$ relative to $v_2$ stems from the combination of initial geometric anisotropy and these dynamical influences. Furthermore, the correlation between $v_3$ and event multiplicity aligns better with a linear dependence on eccentricity $\varepsilon_2$ rather than $v_2$. These results highlight that initial geometry, viscous damping, and non-equilibrium phenomena all play significant roles in anisotropic flow. Consequently, models relying solely on initial geometry to predict $v_3$ are insufficient, as non-equilibrium processes can reduce $v_3$ more significantly than damping alone. Given that $v_3$ is a leading-order anisotropy driven by triangular geometric anisotropy, future research should prioritize enhancing the accuracy of initial state models to better describe $v_3$ and its correlations with other event-shape variables. This study underscores the necessity of simultaneously considering initial geometry, viscous damping, and non-equilibrium effects when analyzing anisotropic flow. Such a comprehensive approach is vital for investigating the transport properties of the quark-gluon plasma through higher-order anisotropic flows, particularly $v_3$ and its harmonics. Ultimately, this holistic perspective is essential for assessing the validity of parton-parton scattering cross-sections within quark and gluon relaxation-time models. This study introduces a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter designed for managing sensor administration on a partially grid-based battlefield. The underlying birth process incorporates a linear transition density with wrap-around characteristics, modeled as a discrete distribution on a grid. Consequently, the proposed PMBM filter with partially grid-oriented birth (PG-O) is also a discrete distribution defined on the battlefield grid. Unlike conventional PMBM filters that rely on birth, motion, and measurement models for each specific entity, this approach utilizes a probability mass function (PMF) for the unknown distribution across the battlefield grid, thereby reducing the number of required models. The paper details the derivation of the PMFM-PG-O filter and the corresponding updates for the PMF-PG-O. Simulation results demonstrate that the new PMBM filter with PG-O converges faster than traditional PMBM filters regarding mean squared error (MSE) on the battlefield grid and offers significant advantages in sensor administration scenarios. Additionally, real-world simulations confirm the effectiveness of both the PMF-PG-O and the PMBM filter with PG-O in sensor administration. Finally, this work provides a detailed account of sensor administration on a partially grid-oriented battlefield and outlines future research directions in this area. Keywords: Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter; point process; Bernoulli process; multi-target tracking; probability mass function (PMF); sensor administration; battlefield; simulations; simulations with real data.

Soccer managers frequently face difficult decisions regarding player substitutions, particularly in the final stages when their team is trailing. While these moments are emotionally charged, they offer ideal conditions for applying reinforcement learning (RL) to optimize substitution tactics. This study introduces a novel hierarchical DQN algorithm, termed H-DQN, designed to enhance in-game strategies for soccer teams. The proposed framework consists of two components: a policy network responsible for determining the optimal moment for a substitution, and an agent tasked with selecting the best specific player. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on a static environment model, our method innovatively trains the environment using game-specific data. Experimental results from the 2018/2019 Bundesliga season demonstrate that teams utilizing the learned H-DQN policy would have recorded higher scores and achieved better outcomes according to multiple reward functions. Furthermore, when tested on match data from the 2017 Champions League knockout stage, the optimized substitution policies consistently outperformed the original decision-making in those critical games. Beyond this specific league, the FRL-SPORTS open-source repository makes the code and datasets for both the 2018/2019 Bundesliga and the 2017 Champions League accessible for further research. Additionally, this work introduces a public dataset derived from the 2019/2020 Bundesliga season. The source code and data for the 2018/2019 and 2017 Champions League studies are available at https://github.com/AhmedElshafiey/FRL_SPORTS, while materials for the 2019/2020 study can be found at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/100X71r0000000000000000000000000?usp=sharing.

This study addresses the control of a single laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV) with a limited field of view to acquire 2D measurements for a vibrating surface. By integrating a linear stage, the LDV's trajectory is managed to cover the entire surface, enabling 2D data collection without requiring dual LDVs or other alternative methods. The proposed approach involves optimizing the LDV's path to gather data from the largest possible area within a fixed timeframe. Simultaneously, a feedback mechanism guides the linear stage to steer the LDV toward an optimal trajectory. The goal is to maximize surface coverage while ensuring the stage remains within its operational limits. An iterative method is developed to determine the best LDV trajectory and corresponding linear stage movements. Validation of this technique is performed using a single-point LDV system to measure a rectangular panel, with results compared against a theoretical 2D LDV system. Additionally, the iterative algorithm is applied to various surface geometries, including a turbine airfoil and a helicopter blade, to demonstrate its versatility. The findings indicate that this distant control method yields results comparable to direct control, effectively covering the target surface area within the specified timeframe. The iterative approach for determining optimal trajectories for different geometries is confirmed to be effective and efficient. This method holds significant value for industries dealing with complex geometries, such as aerospace, where direct two-axis LDV systems are costly and difficult to implement. The proposed solution offers a practical and economical alternative for obtaining two-dimensional vibration data. This paper reports on the application of contextualized language models to detect diachronic semantic shifts, a task that has recently attracted significant attention from researchers utilizing these models. We conducted experiments with BERT, RoBERTa, and the OpenAI GPT-2 model to identify semantic changes in Polish, Croatian, and German. The results indicate that contextualized models are not necessarily effective at detecting semantic changes in low-resource languages, as they tend to generate predictions that rely more on lexical features than on genuine contextual understanding. Given the current findings, we advise against using contextualized models for automatic detection of semantic changes in low-resource languages without further validation. Instead, we propose a simple, effective method for identifying potential semantic changes in low-resource languages that does not depend on contextualized models. Our experiments confirm that this approach yields comparable results to those of contextualized models. Furthermore, we observed that the TREC classifier, a traditional multi-class text classifier, is particularly effective at distinguishing between existing and new uses of words. Finally, we conclude by discussing the potential of contextualized models for verifying human-generated hypotheses regarding semantic changes. The source code for this project is accessible at: https://github.com/AgataRutkowska/Contextualized-Linguistics. Ultimately, this project serves as a case study illustrating the challenges of employing deep learning methods in linguistics and highlighting the risks of blindly applying state-of-the-art techniques to solve specific problems. We emphasize that the suitability of a method for a given task must be empirically verified, as a technique that excels in one area may not be appropriate for another. Ultimately, this project functions as a case study demonstrating the difficulties of utilizing deep learning approaches in linguistics and underscoring the dangers of adopting state-of-the-art methods without empirical validation for specific problems. Specifically, we argue that the appropriateness of a method for a particular task requires empirical confirmation, as a technique successful in one context may not be suitable for another.

We present a Monte Carlo method for simulating the wave function of driven quantum harmonic oscillators, a system characterized by a time-dependent force. Although such systems are analytically solvable, our approach is designed to handle more complex driven quantum systems where exact solutions are unattainable. This technique employs a Metropolis algorithm to evaluate matrix elements between imaginary time states via numerical integration along the imaginary time dimension. The resulting wave function Monte Carlo method offers a straightforward and adaptable framework applicable to various driven quantum systems. We validate this approach using numerical integration and demonstrate that it yields the ground state for undriven oscillators and a time-dependent excited state for driven scenarios. Furthermore, we derive an explicit expression for the ground state of the quantum harmonic oscillator and its corresponding wave function. Distinct from standard Metropolis simulations of many-body systems that generate many-body thermal states, this method produces either a ground state or a time-dependent excited state, depending on the boundary conditions imposed. This distinction arises because the many-body thermal state is a mixture of multiple ground and excited states. Consequently, this wave function Monte Carlo method provides a direct means to calculate expectation values of operators within either a ground state or a time-dependent excited state. Additionally, we can construct the Wigner function for the ground state or time-dependent excited state and perform quasi-probability Monte Carlo simulations of non-commuting operators, such as position and momentum. Ultimately, this technique enables us to compute expectation values of commuting and non-commuting operators for both ground and time-dependent excited states through Monte Carlo simulations of the wave function and Wigner function. Potential applications include simulating quantum interference effects in a quantum Lévy flight, where the ground state or time-dependent excited state interferes with itself, and modeling quantum phenomena in Bose-Einstein condensates. To achieve this, we can simulate the superposition of the ground state and a time-dependent excited state, effectively creating a quantum analog of a water wave. Ultimately, this framework allows for the simulation of various quantum effects, including the uncertainty principle, quantum tunneling, and the Heisenberg uncertainty relation, within the ground state and time-dependent excited state of the quantum harmonic oscillator. We introduce a calculus for reasoning about the probabilistic quantum behaviors of programs that utilize expectations, a technique for probabilistic program verification. By integrating Hoare logic with logic of expectations, this approach enables the specification and analysis of quantum program behaviors through a calculus of expectations. Distinct from traditional Hoare logic, which focuses on boolean assertions, the logic of expectations offers a more granular method for describing quantum program behaviors via linear functionals of Born measurements. Consequently, the verification of quantum programs via the logic of expectations is as effective as behavior characterization through quantum process matrices. Unlike existing approaches that combine separation logic with quantum process matrices for behavioral characterization, our method of reasoning with expectations aligns with the style of probabilistic separation logic while providing a more detailed behavioral description than standard separation logic. Furthermore, our approach of combining a calculus of expectations with a predicate-hyperproperty style of reasoning surpasses recent methods that pair quantum process matrices with first-order hyperproperties for behavioral characterization. The calculus of expectations for probabilistic programs serves as an extension of prior work on probabilistic relational Hoare calculi, incorporating behavioral characterization through a calculus of Born measurements. Similarly, our calculus for quantum programs is an expansion of previous relational Hoare calculus research for quantum programs, also relying on a behavioral characterization based on Born measurements. Although the concepts of separating expectations and Born measurements are originally defined for probabilistic and classical programs respectively, we generalize these notions to apply to both probabilistic and quantum programs. Furthermore, we establish that the calculus of expectations for quantum programs is a conservative extension of its counterpart for probabilistic programs, which in turn extends the relational Hoare calculus for probabilistic programs. Finally, we demonstrate that the relational HOV logic for verifying deep compositionality in probabilistic programs is a conservative extension of our calculus of expectations for probabilistic programs, and we introduce a comparable logic for deep compositionality based on process matrices for quantum programs. As a conservative extension of the relational HOV logic, our calculus of expectations for probabilistic programs inherits its soundness and completeness, and likewise, our calculus of expectations for quantum programs inherits soundness and completeness from the relational HOV logic with process matrices. Additionally, we provide a constructive proof showing that the behavioral characterization by Born measurements for quantum programs is equivalent to quantum process matrices, a result that implies the behavioral characterization by Born measurements for probabilistic programs is equivalent to that by distribution traces. This study addresses the underrepresentation of vector field values near 90 degrees in inferred solar magnetic data, a phenomenon that emerges when maximum entropy methods are used to determine the ambiguity resolution function (ARF) for underdetermined measurements. We demonstrate that this bias is an artifact of the inference process itself, rather than a flaw in the selected metric for the $B_z$ component. Consequently, this bias does not necessarily indicate that the maximum entropy principle is unsuitable for solar vector magnetic field applications. Furthermore, we present a straightforward technique to eliminate this bias by explicitly defining the ARF without relying on automatic determination. Finally, we offer a simple metric for evaluating the degree of underdetermination in specific regions of solar images. For any finite classical group $G$ acting on a vector space $V$, we define and examine the lattice $\mathcal{B}(V)$ consisting of the boolean subgroups generated by invertible diagonal matrices. Our findings demonstrate that this lattice is atomic, distributive, and graded, with its rank corresponding to the product of the dimensions of $V$ and the order of $G$ divided by $|GL_2(\mathbb{F})|$, where $\mathbb{F}$ represents the underlying field. Additionally, we characterize the atoms and elements of rank two within this lattice. These characteristics are utilized to provide a complete description of boolean subgroups of $G$ that are isomorphic to $B_3$, $A_4$, $S_3\times S_2$, $D_8$, $C_3\times C_2$, $C_4\times C_2$, and $C_2\times C_2\times C_2$. Furthermore, we establish that the lattice $\mathcal{B}(V)$ is IS-limited if and only if the product of $|G|$ and the dimension of $V$ does not exceed six, a result that yields a novel proof of a theorem by Aschenbrenner, Baker, and Mildenberger regarding the IS-limited nature of $G$'s inversion subgroups. The completeness of the lattice of boolean diagonal subgroups also offers a fresh characterization of classical groups via their root systems. Furthermore, for the symplectic group $Sp_{2n}(q)$, we identify the maximal subgroup that is not a boolean diagonal subgroup, a discovery with significant implications for the study of maximal subgroups of classical groups. These results contribute to the understanding of invertible subgroups defined by specific matrices, particularly sparse ones, across various areas of group theory.

This paper introduces a novel loss function designed to tackle the challenge of underperforming minority classes in image recognition tasks. The proposed approach integrates a weighting mechanism with the standard loss function, aiming to amplify the contribution of misclassified samples from underrepresented groups during training. Extensive experiments were conducted across three public datasets: MNIST, EMNIST, and Fashion-MNIST. Results indicate that the new loss function significantly boosts classification accuracy for minority categories without compromising overall performance. When compared against state-of-the-weighted loss methods, the proposed function consistently delivered superior accuracy across all categories on every dataset tested. Furthermore, these experiments confirm that the effectiveness of this approach is independent of the underlying network architecture. Beyond classification accuracy, the study also evaluates other performance metrics, including F1-score, Geometric Mean, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient. We introduce ATOMIC, a comprehensive atlas of machine common knowledge supporting if-then reasoning across natural language. By integrating multiple knowledge representations, ATOMIC expands the scope of possible inferences by converting existing common knowledge graphs into if-then reasoning triples. To achieve this, we developed a system that infers additional triples from various knowledge sources to fill in antecedents, thereby creating an atlas of inferred common knowledge. This system employs a neural model trained on inferring if-then triples from natural language, utilizing a large-scale dataset of such triples we generated from existing datasets designed for teaching if-then reasoning in natural language. Evaluation results demonstrate that our system can infer if-then triples to verify human-written natural language inference rules, enabling the verification of common knowledge graphs and graphs of natural language rules. Furthermore, a human study confirms that these inferred if-then triples align with human expectations. The open-source ATOMIC atlas and all associated systems and datasets are available at https://atomic-alignments.org/.

This study introduces a novel method for point cloud video forecasting that tackles the challenge of generating unseen sensor data for specific target points from video input. Unlike traditional approaches that convert video frames into fixed-dimensional vectors using ResNet for regression, our framework employs a hybrid regression strategy. The method comprises two main components: a shared regression module and a task-specific regression module. The task-specific component utilizes a dual representation for point cloud videos, integrating both global and local perspectives. The rapid spread of SARS-CoV-19 has driven the creation of various mathematical models to forecast epidemic trajectories, evaluate intervention strategies, and estimate epidemiological parameters. Galaxy luminosity functions exhibit peaks and turnovers at specific masses, a pattern that theoretically should extend to star formation rate (SFR) distributions. While the double-sloped distribution at low masses is well-established and attributed to the coexistence of star-forming and quiescent galaxies, the existence of a similar turnover at high masses remains uncertain. This study examines the double-sloped distribution across galaxies with log(M*) < 10.5 and identifies a potential turnover for log(M*) > 10.5, suggesting a three-sloped distribution. However, this finding may be influenced by the increasing dominance of bulges in galaxies as mass rises. We hypothesize that bulge dominance creates an apparent saturation of the passive slope for log(M*) > 10.5, masking the actual turnover of star-forming galaxies. To test this, we developed a method to isolate the SFR distribution of bulgeless galaxies and confirmed a turnover at log(M*) = 10.5. Motivated by the persistence of this turnover even when restricting analysis to bulgeless galaxies, we conclude that bulges do not cause the turnover. Finally, we evaluated two mechanisms responsible for this high-mass saturation: a reduction in gas availability and an increase in gas outflows. Our results indicate that outflows are unlikely to be the primary driver, as the required outflow efficiency would need to be unreasonably high. Furthermore, we find that the turnover occurs at a mass where gas fractions are already low, suggesting that gas depletion is the dominant mechanism causing the turnover. To validate this, we developed a simple model incorporating depletion times, initial mass functions, and the main sequence slope, successfully reproducing the observed distribution of bulgeless galaxies. Looking ahead, future research should focus on refining the measurement of the turnover and investigating the roles of mergers and the transition from rapid to slow star formation. Additionally, determining the anisotropy of outflows and their impact on the global star formation history of log(M*) > 10.5 galaxies remain important areas for further study. This work introduces the Transformation-Point Cloud (TPC) structure, a memory-efficient method designed to store and index point cloud data. By integrating the TPC structure with a universal outlier detection technique, we present a novel approach for identifying anomalies in point cloud structures. Specifically, we combine TPC with a uniqueness-based smoothing strategy called Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TUS) to create an index for processing offline large-scale point cloud datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively detects anomalies within point cloud structures and performs superior outlier detection compared to existing techniques when utilizing the Teaser, Testbed, and Wild datasets. Furthermore, the integration of TPC and TUS offers significant memory savings over traditional Point Cloud (PC) storage, while our anomaly detection framework delivers better performance than current methods across various datasets. The source code for this project is accessible at: https://github.com/Anomaly-Detection-Lab/TPC-Structure-Index-For-Point-Cloud-Structure-Outlier-Detection.

This paper presents a geometric framework for evaluating semantic properties of programs, encompassing both static analysis techniques like type systems and testing methods. Within this framework, various program semantics are modeled as sheaves defined over a specific topological space termed the "failure space," which systematically represents all potential program failures. Consequently, different semantics can be directly compared to assess the strengths and limitations of corresponding static and dynamic approaches. The framework also introduces a "guarantee space" to quantify the quality of static properties and outlines a methodology for optimizing test suites based on coverage. As a demonstration, the work defines a family of semantics ranging from fully operationalistic to completely static, offering a unified perspective on diverse static and dynamic semantic properties. Furthermore, it proposes a meta-type system capable of certifying a range of inter-type refinement relations. Finally, a methodology is described for enhancing test suites to cover all feasible operationalistic properties, with concrete examples provided to illustrate these concepts in action. The proposed framework serves as a versatile tool for comparing and optimizing both static and dynamic program properties, potentially guiding the development of new static properties and technologies. The underlying theory is detailed in this paper, while the associated software implementation will be released as open source.

This study introduces a framework for precisely identifying incipient shear bands in uniaxially loaded glass fiber-reinforced vinyl ester self-sensing composites via an electrical impedance tomography (EIT) technique termed exact-image EIT. To achieve this, a global optimization-based algorithm named genetic direct search (GDS) was developed specifically for damage localization. The resulting exact images of anisotropic damage formation are derived from the conductivity tensor field using a nonlinear inverse method called iteratively regularized least-squares (IRLS). Findings indicate that the GDS algorithm successfully determined the optimal conductivity tensor field to produce visually intuitive exact images of incipient shear band localization. These results validate the efficacy of the exact-image IRl method in generating intuitive tensor field maps that accurately depict incipient shear bands. Furthermore, it was observed that once a shear band forms, a significant portion of the composite experiences a macroscopic drop in conductivity, causing the "undamaged" regions outside the band to act as a linear background. Consequently, a conventional linear image method, the filtered Natterer algorithm (FNA), was employed to image incipient shear bands after initial damage occurred. The FNA successfully generated accurate images of the bands, confirming the validity of the exact-image EIT approach. Ultimately, the proposed framework of exact-image EIT holds significant value for investigating the mechanisms of progressive damage, as it enables the precise imaging of damage formation beyond simple localization phenomena.

Finally, we apply these formulations to determine the volume of several particular domains. These regions include the interior of a hyper-sphere, the sector of a hyper-sphere, the zone of a hyper-sphere, and the tetrahedron defined by a trihedral angle and a trihedral sector. Furthermore, we leverage these results to derive the tensor form of the trihedral angle element solid. The findings presented here may find utility in investigations concerning the "direction" operator and the "zone" operator when applied to Fock spaces constructed from Euclidean spaces. Such research holds significant relevance for the study of hyperspherical coordinates and their associated creation and annihilation operators within Fock spaces, which in turn could impact investigations into the geometric formulation of quantum mechanics. Additionally, these results could serve the field of mathematical statistics, particularly in analyses involving directional statistics and hyperspherical coordinates. Regarding the classification of this work, the primary Subject Area is Mathematics (math), with the specific subfield being Metric Geometry (math.MG). The key takeaways from this report are: this paper derives the tensor expressions for the area element of hyper-spheres in Euclidean spaces, which can be applied to calculate the volume of various regions; these derivations could benefit research on the "direction" and "zone" operators in Euclidean Fock spaces, potentially influencing the geometric approach to quantum mechanics; and these calculations may also assist mathematical statistics, specifically in the study of directional statistics.

High-dimensional matrix inversion is crucial for numerous applications, including statistical analysis, machine learning, and signal processing. This report introduces a novel method for accelerating iterative matrix inversion by extending the Frobenius-Elevated and Cauchy-Elevated Techniques. While these traditional approaches are detailed in this work for the first time with explicit algorithms, the proposed technique offers a significant speedup of approximately a factor of $2.32$ compared to the Frobenius-Elevated Method and a factor of $1.73$ against the Cauchy-Elevated Technique. Furthermore, this new method is inherently more efficient than both earlier approaches. Given that the standard iterative inversion relies on Conjugate Gradient (CG) iteration, this paper defines a generalized form of the CG iteration as the "Generalized Conjugate Gradient (GCG) Iteration." The proposed solution combines an order-3 elevated method with GCG iterations; alternatively, lower-order elevated techniques paired with GCG iterations can also be implemented. Ultimately, this approach surpasses all current methods, including direct inversion strategies like Coulomb, Bidiagonalization, and Chebyshev techniques, as well as previous elevated-order methods. The implementation utilizes CUDA, and a comparative analysis with other iterative methods is provided. Furthermore, this work establishes a framework for future elevated-order techniques, potentially yielding further speed improvements. The combination of the order-3 method and the generalizable elevated-order framework could prove valuable in various fields, such as physics, for large-scale simulations. All proposed methods are applicable to both real and complex matrices. The source code for this implementation is accessible at: https://github.com/Aniruddha-Sen/Elevated-Order-Techniques-for-Iterative-Matrix-Inversion-for-GPU-Acceleration. The findings indicate that while the VSI remains stable in optically thin regions, the growth rate of instabilities in the inner zone rises as dust accumulation intensifies. Conversely, in the outer zone, dust accumulation suppresses instability growth. Once the vertical turbulent viscosity surpasses $10^{-9}$, other instabilities, such as the gravitational instability, are expected to dominate. These results suggest that the early phase of dust accumulation in the outer regions will likely occur under laminar flow conditions, whereas the inner regions will experience turbulent mixing driven by VSI. Consequently, dust accumulation in the outer regions will be governed by aerodynamic mechanisms, whereas both aerodynamic forces and VSI will drive accumulation in the inner regions. This paper introduces Global Mean Pooling (GMP) as a replacement for dynamic entrance layers in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) designed for video classification tasks. By substituting the GMP layer for the initial frame pooling operation, the model gains the ability to process videos of variable lengths without requiring a fixed dimension. The proposed architecture, termed GMP-Net, eliminates the need for dynamic layers, thereby simplifying the network structure and enhancing computational efficiency. Extensive experiments conducted on two public datasets, UCF-101 and HMDB-51, confirm that GMP-Net outperforms existing state-of-the methods. Furthermore, the model demonstrates robustness when trained and tested on videos of differing lengths. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/GMP-Net. Ultimately, this work offers a novel perspective on handling videos of variable duration through the GMP layer, which holds significant potential for future research. Keywords: Convolutional Neural Network, Video Classification, Global Mean Pooling, Dynamic Entrance Layer, UCF-101, HMDB-51.

This study introduces Random Stroll for Education (RfE), a novel approach to model training for Federated Learning (FL) systems serving clients with non-independent and identically distributed (NIDID) data. By leveraging a lightweight data exploration algorithm, RfE enables a central model to learn from data volumes that would otherwise be insufficient for individual clients. The combination of the data exploration algorithm and the central model constitutes an Educated Model (EM). Unlike the traditional model updated at the conclusion of each iteration, the EM is updated at every step to guide the selection of local training data for each client. We evaluated RfE using the English Language Learning (ELL) dataset, a real-world scenario involving students accessing an educational mobile application. The results indicate that for the specific ELL dataset, the Random Stroll algorithm effectively identifies high-quality data, and the RfE method achieves superior accuracy compared to standard data sampling techniques. Furthermore, RfE significantly reduces the data processing time per iteration for each client. These findings suggest that Random Stroll is an effective data exploration strategy for similar datasets, offering a viable solution to expand training data for underrepresented samples and enhancing the performance of educational models within FL environments. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Aniruddha1999/RfE.

Consistency regularization remains a dominant approach for unlabeled medical image segmentation, relying on the expectation that predictions for augmented versions of the same input should align. However, existing methods often lack sufficient expressiveness to effectively leverage the semantic richness inherent in medical imaging. This paper introduces a novel consistency regularization framework grounded in the "region of support" concept from the AWAARD language. By utilizing this region, our approach guides the network to ensure that the probability mass within the region of support of an image matches that of its augmented counterpart. We validate this method, termed Region of Support Regularization (RoSR), across three medical image segmentation datasets. Results demonstrate that RoSR outperforms state-of-the-art consistency regularization techniques, yielding a 2.1% improvement in mean teacher regularization and a 1.9% gain in mean labeled consistency regularization on one dataset. Furthermore, RoSR exhibits remarkable robustness against adversarial attacks and maintains high performance even when trained on noisy labels. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/aw-ml-langs/rosr.

This study introduces a method and hardware architecture for LSTM networks optimized for video identification systems. Unlike conventional approaches that focus solely on model training, our strategy employs system-level co-design to balance the energy demands of both the video identification application and the supporting LSTM architecture. This study examines the Schr\"odinger equation defined on the exterior of a convex obstacle within $\R^{2}$, subject to a nonlinear boundary condition. It is demonstrated that the classical solution blows up in finite time under the assumption of a mass supercritical nonlinearity. Furthermore, it is proven that solutions existing globally in time exhibit asymptotic stability for small initial data. These findings extend previous research by offering a simpler proof of finite-time blowup for boundary nonlinearities of the form $\lambda |u|^{p-1}u$ where $p < 3$, and by establishing global existence for data sizes smaller than a specific threshold dependent on the geometry of the obstacle. The analysis further reveals that the global existence of solutions is contingent upon the curvature of the boundary when the nonlinearity is weak.

Hypothesis testing in statistics relies on two primary methodologies: p-values and Bayes factors. While the scientific community has long advocated for Bayes factors as a complement to significance testing, their practical application has been limited. This limitation stems from the widespread belief that Bayes factors are overly sensitive to prior choices, a characteristic that appears to contradict their goal of offering an objective measure of evidence. In this paper, we challenge this assumption, arguing that Bayes factors can be employed more effectively if specific strategies are adopted regarding both the selection of priors and the computation of the factors themselves. Achieving these goals requires a tailored approach. We begin by clarifying the source of the sensitivity problem and outlining the necessary conditions for its resolution. Subsequently, we introduce two distinct strategies for incorporating domain knowledge into the priors used for effect size parameters within the calculation of Bayes factors. This study introduces DiscSense, a system designed to evaluate the performance of classifiers tasked with identifying and classifying discourse markers. Unlike previous evaluations that primarily focused on whether a linking expression between two sentences received the correct label, DiscSense offers a granular, automated assessment of both detection and classification across various linguistic categories. The outcome of this examination serves as a metric for the combination of precision and recall, referred to as the "sense" for each category. To achieve this, we developed a detailed taxonomy for discourse markers and created two manual classification guidelines: one for determining the presence or absence of a marker and another for assigning its category when present. These guidelines were applied to the pairs of consecutive sentences from the discourse marker datasets SEMEVAL 2014 (Task 4) and ChAMELEON. When compared against the winning teams' predictions from SEMEVAL 2014 and ChAMELEON using the traditional F1 score, there was no significant improvement in overall performance. However, the granular sense-based evaluation reveals that the predictions from these top-performing systems contain numerous errors in specific categories, indicating that the highest F1 scores do not necessarily reflect accurate classification. To facilitate future research, we have made the DiscSense system, the taxonomy, and both classification guidelines available as open resources at https://github.com/linguistICT/DiscSense. Additionally, we developed a similar evaluation approach for the classification of utterance acts within the ChAMELEON dataset, for which we also created a dedicated system and set of guidelines. This study introduces a one-parameter family of generalized Jordanian twists, demonstrating that they modify only the boundary conditions of quantum field theories. This paper addresses the challenge of deciding inclusion between deterministic finite automata and expressions defined by a regular language grammar. This study introduces a novel architecture for lobster-eye X-ray telescopes, designed to expand both the field of view and effective area beyond the constraints of current systems. This new configuration utilizes a multiplexed arrangement of smaller lobster-eye modules, each equipped with a conventional imaging zone plate at its focal plane to record a compact, high-resolution image of a specific sky sector. The concept is detailed through simulations of a monitor serving a 20,000 square degree field, composed of nine 2,200 square degree sectors. Simulation outcomes indicate that a 90\% field of view with a resolution of 10 arcminutes can be achieved across the 18,000 square degree area covered by the nine modules. Furthermore, the angular resolution within the central field of view of each module can be enhanced to approximately 5 arcminutes by optimizing the interplay between the lobster-eye lens and the imaging zone plate. These simulations confirm that multiplexing lobster-eye lenses is feasible and offers a viable method for broad-field monitoring with uniform resolution. Such a system would be particularly valuable for post-outburst multi-variable observations, enabling rapid identification of variable sources and the rapid deployment of narrow-field instruments to investigate the event's field. Potential applications include rapid response to X-ray transients detected by wide-field monitors like NEUTRON Star X-ray INstrument (NIXI) on the IXPE satellite or the Imager for X-ray Astrophysics Satellite (IXAS) on the STIXI satellite, as well as pre- and post-event observations of astronomical phenomena by other telescopes. Feasibility simulations for this architecture are conducted using the open-source Monte Carlo ray-tracing code, GEANT4.9.x.

We demonstrate a local magnetic field measurement technique for an atomic interferometer that exploits the Meissner effect of a superconductor to detect field variations rather than absolute values. Furthermore, this technique can enhance the precision of local field sensing in atomic interferometric gyroscopes and accelerometers. The described method is referred to as the LIFM technique (local magnetic field measurement via local field expulsion).

We examine the fundamental particle physics characteristics of the minimal scoto-seesaw model, addressing both neutrino phenomena and wider dark sector issues. While prior research concentrated on addressing the light neutrino mass mechanism via the seesaw and enhancing the Higgs vacuum stability, this work investigates the basic phenomenology of direct dark sector scattering. Specifically, we analyze the mass matrix for the additional scalar and seesaw neutrino states, detailing the conditions required for a viable dark matter mass spectrum. Furthermore, we explore the simplest dark matter direct detection scenarios, outlining the necessary constraints on parameters and comparing them with those from indirect detection. Finally, we present a comprehensive study of collider signatures, focusing on the production and decay of the H-like particle. Complementing these investigations, we map out the model's parameter space by examining neutrino oscillation data, direct dark matter detection limits, LHC constraints, and theoretical boundaries. Our findings indicate that although the model is highly constrained, it remains feasible, with the ultimate limits on the sterile neutrino mass matrix arising from a combination of direct detection and collider experiments. Our detailed examination of these phenomena offers valuable insights for future research into simple dark matter extension models.
